summary: Describes the control plane and Mapping Service for LISP, implemented by Map-Resolvers and Map-Servers, which provide a simplified front end to databases mapping endpoint IDs to routing locators. It obsoletes RFC 6830 and RFC 6833. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: LISP keeps the addresses a site uses separate from the addresses of the network that carries its traffic, so something has to track which of them is in use where. This RFC defines the two helpers that do that work, the messages they exchange, and how a registration is proved genuine.

questions: what are lisp map-resolvers and map-servers
how does lisp map eids to rlocs
subtitle: The helpers that answer "where does this address live now?" and the messages they exchange over UDP port 4342.

tldr.problem: LISP splits the addresses used by IP into endpoint identifiers used inside sites and routing locators used on the transit networks, so routers need to learn which locators currently serve a given endpoint.
tldr.mechanism: Map-Resolvers answer lookups for ingress routers and Map-Servers publish the mappings that egress routers register, using Map-Request, Map-Reply, Map-Register and Map-Notify messages carried in UDP on port 4342.
tldr.outcome: Routers talk to a simple front end rather than to a mapping database, which keeps the database design swappable and lowers the cost of deploying LISP. This document obsoletes RFC 6830 and RFC 6833.

today: RFC 9301 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2022. It obsoletes RFC 6830 and RFC 6833, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why LISP Needs a Control Plane
sections.content:
LISP, described in RFC 9300, separates the addresses currently used by IP into two namespaces. Endpoint IDs (EIDs) are used within sites. Routing Locators (RLOCs) are used on the transit networks that make up the Internet. To make the separation work, LISP needs a way of mapping an EID to an RLOC, and it assumes a database that stores those mappings and spreads them across the nodes of a mapping system. Several such databases have been proposed, among them LISP-NERD, LISP-ALT and LISP-DDT.

The Mapping Service defined here has two kinds of device. A Map-Resolver accepts Map-Requests from an Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR) and resolves the mapping using a database. A Map-Server learns authoritative mappings from an Egress Tunnel Router (ETR) and publishes them in a database. Map-Servers share basic configuration and maintenance properties with DNS servers, and Map-Resolvers are conceptually similar to DNS caching resolvers, so the RFC borrows that terminology.

The same control plane can sit on top of several data planes, including LISP itself, LISP-GPE, VXLAN, GRE, GTP, Identifier-Locator Addressing and Segment Routing. The RFC also says plainly that LISP is not meant to solve connectivity and scaling problems for arbitrary communicating parties.

For use over the public Internet the RFC sets two rules. LISP Security (LISP-SEC, RFC 9303) MUST be implemented, which means the S-bit MUST be set in Map-Reply, Map-Register and Encapsulated Control Messages. Implementations SHOULD use HMAC-SHA256-128+HKDF-SHA256 as the Algorithm ID in a Map-Register, and MUST NOT use None or HMAC-SHA-1-96-None there.
sections.plainLanguage: LISP splits an address into two: one that says which device it is, and one that says where the device is attached. A database and two kinds of helper keep the two in step.

sections.title: Map-Servers and Map-Resolvers
sections.content:
A Map-Server publishes EID-Prefixes in a LISP mapping database on behalf of a set of ETRs. To publish, an ETR periodically sends Map-Register messages that list the EID-Prefixes it owns together with the RLOCs that can be used to reach it. When the Map-Server receives a Map-Request, it consults the database to find an ETR that can answer with the set of RLOCs for the requested prefix.

How the database is reached depends on which one is in use. With LISP-ALT, a Map-Server connects to the ALT network and acts as a last-hop ALT-Router; intermediate ALT-Routers forward Map-Requests to the Map-Server that advertises the prefix, and the Map-Server forwards them on to the owning ETR. With LISP-DDT, the Map-Server sends the final Map-Referral messages of the Delegated Database Tree.

A Map-Resolver receives Encapsulated Map-Requests from its client ITRs and uses a mapping database system to find the right ETR to answer them. On a LISP-ALT network it acts as a first-hop ALT-Router, with GRE tunnels to other ALT-Routers and BGP used to learn paths to ETRs. On a LISP-DDT network it keeps a referral cache and acts as a first-hop DDT node.

In this specification Map-Resolvers work in a non-caching mode only: they decapsulate Encapsulated Map-Requests and forward them. Caching is out of scope. A single device can implement both the Map-Server and the Map-Resolver functions, and often does.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper receives the registrations that say which prefixes a site owns. The other helper answers the queries that ask where an address is now.

sections.title: The Control Message Formats
sections.content:
All control messages travel in UDP. A Map-Request, a Map-Register, and a Map-Notify used as a notification are sent to destination port 4342 from a source port the sender picks. A Map-Reply, a Map-Notify used as an acknowledgment, and a Map-Notify-Ack come from source port 4342. Implementations MUST accept packets when either port is 4342, because a NAT may change the port number. The UDP checksum is set to non-zero and MUST be checked on receipt; a message that fails is dropped. Where the path MTU of the underlying network is unknown, messages MUST be limited to 576 bytes for IPv4 or 1280 bytes for IPv6, counting the whole IP packet.

A Map-Request (type 1) asks for a mapping. It carries an 8-octet random nonce, an optional source EID, one or more ITR-RLOC addresses that the reply can be sent to, and the EID-Prefix being asked about. Senders MUST include one record only, and Map-Requests MUST be rate limited to 1 per second per EID-Prefix. After 10 retransmits with no Map-Reply, the sender MUST wait 30 seconds.

A Map-Reply (type 2) echoes the nonce and returns records. Each record holds a TTL in minutes, an EID-Prefix and a locator set. Every locator has a Priority, where lower values are preferred and 255 means the locator must not be used for unicast, and a Weight that splits traffic between locators of equal priority. When prefixes overlap, the most specific match for the requested EID comes back in a single reply. A reply with an empty locator set is a Negative Map-Reply, and its action code says what the requester should do next.

A Map-Register (type 3) publishes records, a Map-Notify (type 4) acknowledges a registration, and a Map-Notify-Ack (type 5) acknowledges an unsolicited Map-Notify. An Encapsulated Control Message (type 8) wraps another control message: an outer IP header using RLOC addresses, an outer UDP header to port 4342, then an inner header that may use EID addresses. Port number 4341 MUST NOT be used, and a Map-Request used as a reachability probe MUST NOT be sent inside an encapsulated message.
sections.plainLanguage: A query, a reply, a registration, an acknowledgment, and a wrapper for carrying one of these. Each type has a fixed number in its header, so a receiver knows what it has been sent.

sections.title: Authenticating Registrations
sections.content:
Map-Register messages are authenticated so that a Map-Server publishes only what a trusted ETR sent. The ETR and the Map-Server share a pre-shared secret, which MUST be unique for each LISP Site-ID. The Key ID field names the secret in use, which lets secrets be rotated without disruption, and the Algorithm ID field names the pair of key derivation function and message authentication code to use.

The per-message key is derived from the nonce and the secret, with a salt that depends on the message type: Map-Register Authentication, Map-Notify Authentication or Map-Notify-Ack Authentication. The message authentication code is then computed over the whole message with the authentication field set to zero. Implementations MUST implement HMAC-SHA-256-128 and SHOULD implement HMAC-SHA-256-128 with HKDF-SHA256.

The Nonce in a Map-Register is incremented with each message. A Map-Server MUST save the last nonce for each ETR xTR-ID and key pair in persistent storage, and MUST drop a Map-Register whose nonce is not greater, which is what stops an old message being replayed. An ETR that cannot save its nonce MUST use a new authentication key after a restart. When the I-bit is set, a 128-bit xTR-ID and a 64-bit Site-ID are appended to identify the sender and the site it belongs to. A Map-Register, Map-Notify or Map-Notify-Ack whose authentication data fails to validate is dropped without further processing.
sections.plainLanguage: A registration carries a code computed from a secret that only the sender and the receiver share. A counter that grows on every message stops a captured message from being sent again.

sections.title: Keeping Mappings Fresh and Testing Locators
sections.content:
The RFC covers this in two sections. Section 6 is about changing the contents of a mapping, and section 7 is about checking that a locator is still reachable.

ITRs keep a local Map-Cache, so when an ETR changes a mapping, remote ITRs have to find out. The RFC defines the Solicit-Map-Request (SMR) as the control plane push mechanism. It is simply a bit set in a Map-Request. An ETR sends SMRs to the sites it has been sending encapsulated data packets to during the last minute. An ITR that receives an SMR sends its own SMR-invoked Map-Request, and that request MUST go through the mapping system rather than directly. Both sides MUST rate limit these messages, and the RFC recommends no more than one packet every 3 seconds. An ITR with no cached mapping SHOULD NOT send an SMR-invoked request, because it will ask when it next needs to send.

There are also several ways to learn that a locator is down: an ICMP Network Unreachable or Host Unreachable message, a missing route in the underlay routing table, an ICMP Port Unreachable, and a Map-Reply arriving from an ETR. The RFC warns that the ICMP method is unreliable because many network operators turn those messages off. Reachability is never tested with data packets, because that risks losing traffic for end-to-end sessions.

RLOC-Probing is the explicit method. An ITR sends a Map-Request with the probe bit set directly to a locator, not through the mapping system. The ETR answers with a Map-Reply that has the probe bit set, which should carry the current mapping for the prefix. Probing handles many failure cases and gives rough round-trip time estimates, but it costs control messages and bandwidth, especially when failures have to be noticed quickly.
sections.plainLanguage: When a site changes the addresses it serves, it tells the sites it has recently written to, and they look the answer up again. A router can also send a probe straight to an address to see whether it still answers.

sections.title: Resolving and Registering Mappings
sections.content:
An ITR is configured with one or more Map-Resolver addresses. These are RLOCs and MUST be routable on the underlying core network, since resolving them through LISP would be circular. When the ITR has no cached mapping, it sends an Encapsulated Map-Request to a Map-Resolver and can expect one of three answers: an immediate Negative Map-Reply with the action code Natively-Forward and a 15-minute TTL if the resolver knows the EID does not exist; a Negative Map-Reply from a Map-Server for a hole in an authoritative prefix, with a 1-minute TTL when a delegated prefix has no registered ETRs; or a real Map-Reply from the ETR that owns the mapping, or from a Map-Server answering on its behalf.

On the registration side, an ETR sends Map-Register messages periodically, with a suggested interval of one minute. A Map-Server SHOULD remove a registration it has not refreshed within three minutes, and after a restart an ETR MAY register as often as once every 20 seconds for at most five minutes. The ETR and the Map-Server MUST already share a secret, and the Map-Server SHOULD be configured with the list of EID-Prefixes each ETR may register. The Map-Server accepts only the prefixes configured for that ETR, because skipping that check would leave the mapping system open to trivial prefix hijacking. The M-bit asks for a Map-Notify back, and the P-bit asks the Map-Server to answer Map-Requests on the ETR's behalf, in which case the ETR SHOULD list all the RLOCs of all the ETRs for the prefix.

When a Map-Server gets a Map-Request it first checks the destination against its configured prefixes. With no match it returns a Negative Map-Reply with action code Natively-Forward and a 15-minute TTL. It then looks for an ETR that registered the matching prefix, and returns a Negative Map-Reply with a 1-minute TTL if there is none. If a registered ETR asked for proxy replies, the Map-Server answers the request itself. Otherwise it re-encapsulates the request and forwards it to one of the registered ETRs, so the ETR's Map-Reply goes to the RLOC in the Map-Request rather than to the Map-Server.

A Map-Resolver that cannot answer from its own data forwards the unencapsulated request, with the ITR's RLOC as the source, into the mapping database, so the answer also goes straight to the ITR. A Map-Resolver address can be anycast, so each ITR reaches one that is close to it.
sections.plainLanguage: A router with no entry for an address asks its lookup helper. The helper either returns the addresses that serve that prefix, says the prefix is not served, or passes the question to the site that owns it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security section rests on three assumptions: the mapping system is secure and trusted, the ETRs have a preconfigured trust relationship with it that includes a shared secret, and LISP-SEC MUST be implemented. The RFC then lists the threats. The Map-Request and Map-Reply exchange can be used for denial of service and for amplification attacks, which filters and rate limiters mitigate. It can also be used to inject forged mappings into the cache of an ITR, redirecting traffic to the attacker, and a valid ETR can try to overclaim a larger prefix than it owns. LISP-SEC addresses origin authentication, integrity, man-in-the-middle attacks and prefix overclaiming. Deployments worried about manipulated control messages MUST drop messages that carry no LISP-SEC material. Mechanisms to encrypt the control messages SHOULD be deployed, with DTLS and lisp-crypto given as examples.

The privacy section adds a different concern. LISP can use long-lived EIDs that survive a device moving, and those identifiers are bound to RLOCs, which carry the topological location. When control messages are not encrypted, an attacker can often read or query the mappings and then correlate the EID with the RLOC to track a user's location and movement. The RFC suggests access control lists or stronger authentication in the mapping system so that only authorised users can read the mappings, and points to ephemeral EIDs as a way of making tracking harder.
sections.plainLanguage: The mapping system has to keep its records safe from change and its answers private. The RFC requires the security extension, warns about forged lookups, and points out that long-lived identifiers can be followed around the network.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 6830 and RFC 6833
sections.content:
This document replaces RFC 6830 and RFC 6833. The RFC lists the changes that matter to implementers:

  • The 16-bit Key ID field of Map-Register and Map-Notify is split into an 8-bit Key ID and an 8-bit Algorithm ID.
  • A Map-Notify-Ack message is defined to make Map-Notify reliable. Implementations of it already existed before the RFC.
  • The Map-Referral codepoint from LISP-DDT is incorporated.
  • Bits L and D are added to Map-Request, and bits S, I, E, T, a, R and M to Map-Register.
  • Two action values are added to EID-Records: Drop/Policy-Denied and Drop/Auth-Failure.

For IANA, UDP port 4342 is the LISP control plane port, the packet type registry now points to this document, and the Key ID registry is renamed "LISP Algorithm ID Numbers" with four values defined here: None (0), HMAC-SHA-1-96-None (1), HMAC-SHA-256-128-None (2) and HMAC-SHA256-128+HKDF-SHA256 (3). The separate address type registry requested by RFC 6830 is closed in favour of the LCAF types registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The new edition splits one field into two, adds a way to acknowledge an acknowledgment, and registers the algorithm numbers that name the code used to protect a registration.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Message type. The value 1 is a Map-Request.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Authoritative bit: the destination site should answer rather than the mapping database.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: Map-data-present bit: a Map-Reply record is included in the request.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Probe bit: the request tests whether a locator is reachable.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved bits, set to 0 on transmit and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Local-xTR bit: the RLOC is the sender's own IP address.

fields.name: D
fields.desc: Do-not-map-reply bit: the receiver need not answer.

fields.name: IRC
fields.desc: ITR-RLOC count: the number of extra ITR-RLOC address fields, from 0 to 31.

fields.name: Record Count
fields.desc: Number of records. A sender sends one record only.

fields.name: Nonce
fields.desc: Random value copied into the Map-Reply so the request can be matched.

fields.name: Source-EID-AFI
fields.desc: Address family of the source EID address that follows.

fields.name: ITR-RLOC-AFI
fields.desc: Address family of the ITR-RLOC address that follows.

items.label: Map-Request
items.desc: Asks for an EID-to-RLOC mapping, or probes a locator.

items.label: Map-Reply
items.desc: Returns mapping records, or an empty set for a negative reply.

items.label: Map-Register
items.desc: An ETR publishes its EID-Prefixes to a Map-Server.

items.label: Map-Notify
items.desc: Acknowledges a Map-Register, or notifies a change.

items.label: DDT Map-Referral
items.desc: Used by the LISP-DDT mapping system.

items.label: Encapsulated Control Message
items.desc: Wraps another control message, such as a Map-Request.

items.label: Shared Extension Message
items.desc: For experimenting with new message formats.

messages.label: Encapsulated Map-Request
messages.note: Sent to UDP port 4342 when the Map-Cache has no entry.

messages.label: Map-Request
messages.note: Forwarded into the mapping database, with the ITR RLOC as the source address.

messages.label: Encapsulated Map-Request
messages.note: Re-encapsulated and forwarded to one of the registered ETRs.

messages.label: Map-Reply
messages.note: Sent straight to the RLOC in the Map-Request, with the nonce echoed.

viz.caption: AN ETR REGISTERING ITS EID-PREFIXES WITH A MAP-SERVER (ILLUSTRATIVE)

messages.label: Map-Register
messages.note: Authenticated with a key derived from the shared secret. The M-bit asks for a Map-Notify.

messages.label: Map-Notify
messages.note: Copies the Map-Register fields and recomputes the authentication data.

items.title: None, number 0
items.text: No message authentication code and no key derivation function.

items.title: HMAC-SHA-1-96-None, number 1
items.text: The message authentication code from RFC 2404, with no key derivation function.

items.title: HMAC-SHA-256-128-None, number 2
items.text: The message authentication code from RFC 4868, with no key derivation function.

items.title: HMAC-SHA256-128+HKDF-SHA256, number 3
items.text: The message authentication code from RFC 4868 with HKDF-SHA256 key derivation. Implementations must implement HMAC-SHA-256-128 and should implement this one.
